n: Scam compounds and end-to-end scam-proceeds flows
ds: Industrialised online-fraud operations (investment, romance and impersonation scams, including pig-butchering) run from compound-style premises, often staffed by people recruited under false pretences and held in forced labour. The financial footprint spans victim payments, recruited receiving accounts, consolidation, crypto conversion and cash-out, plus corporate fronts and infrastructure spending that sustain the operation. Defensive framing: this entry lists observable financial signals for institutions, not operating methods. See FR-ROM (victim journey) and HT-FORCEDLAB (labour exploitation) for context only.

cn.rt: Recruited mule everyday and savings accounts collect and consolidate scam proceeds before crypto or offshore cash-out.

rat: Victims approached via social and messaging platforms; mule accounts collect and consolidate, then crypto off-ramps or wires abroad.

ind.n: Accounts used as pass-through for overseas scam operations
ind.cx: Recruited or complicit account holders receive victim funds and quickly convert to stablecoins or wire abroad, the core mule step in the compound payment chain.
ind.fp: May have innocent explanations; assess in context of customer profile and other indicators.
ind.ds: recruited accounts receive victim funds and convert quickly to stablecoins or wire abroad.

ind.n: Account receiving funds from multiple apparent fraud victims
ind.cx: A low-activity account receives payments from several apparent investment or romance scam victims, sometimes with narratives referencing a "platform" or "trading".
ind.fp: Legitimate sales, crowdfunding or refunds can look similar; check payment references and account history.
ind.ds: A new or low-activity account receives payments from several unrelated individuals who appear to be victims of fraud or phishing, followed by onward movement or cash-out.

ind.n: Receiving account is new or recently dormant with many unrelated senders
ind.cx: New or reactivated receiving accounts collect payments from unrelated individuals, matching the collection tier that feeds a compound's consolidation accounts.
ind.fp: Fundraising, club accounts or small traders with genuine many-to-one inflows.
ind.ds: Mule-side: a recently opened or reactivated account receives payments from many unrelated people with narratives that do not fit the stated profile.

ind.n: Funds routed to multiple small accounts then consolidated
ind.cx: Victim payments are split across many personal and corporate accounts then consolidated to a small number of accounts or exchange deposits.
ind.fp: Payroll or marketplace payouts with similar structure.
ind.ds: Mule-side: scam proceeds are split across many personal and corporate accounts before consolidation and cash-out.

ind.n: Destination wallet linked to scam or fraud clusters
ind.cx: Victim deposits or onward transfers reach wallet addresses attributed by analytics providers to fake investment platforms or scam clusters.
ind.ds: Receiving address is attributed to investment, romance or impersonation scams.

ind.n: Shared devices, IP addresses or contact details across accounts
ind.cx: Dozens of apparently unrelated receiving or onboarding accounts share devices, IP ranges, phone numbers or documents, indicating one operating group behind many accounts.
ind.fp: Households and shared workplaces share details.
ind.ds: Multiple unrelated accounts share devices, phone numbers, email or addresses.

ind.n: Rapid movement offshore or to crypto after receipt
ind.cx: Scam proceeds leave rapidly to offshore accounts or are converted to virtual assets within hours of credit, the cash-out end of the chain.
ind.fp: Genuine international payments or planned crypto purchases by established customers.
ind.ds: Incoming funds are quickly sent abroad or converted to virtual assets soon after being credited.

ind.n: Funds sent to unlicensed or weakly regulated exchanges
ind.cx: Consolidated proceeds are sent to exchanges, OTC desks or platforms with weak licensing or AML controls, enabling off-ramp into fiat or further layering.
ind.fp: Some legitimate smaller platforms are not yet registered or are licensed in other regimes.
ind.ds: Withdrawals or flows go to exchanges or VASPs that lack licensing or effective AML and sanctions controls.

ind.n: Operating-company profile with scam-infrastructure spending and no business footprint
ind.cx: Front or service companies that fund the physical and technical operation of a compound appear as customers whose spending profile fits infrastructure rather than their declared business.
ind.fp: Legitimate offshore call centres, start-ups, IT outsourcers and marketing firms also spend heavily on infrastructure and may have thin early-stage revenue and remote ownership.
ind.ds: A corporate customer in recruitment, customer-service outsourcing, gaming, crypto or consultancy, often with remote principals, shows spending on bulk telecoms, servers, hosting, domains, devices and accommodation but little revenue, payroll or customer activity consistent with its stated business.

ind.n: Payments by relatives for release or "fees" for a person held abroad
ind.cx: Families of people held in forced labour at a compound may pay demanded sums; the customer can be a victim of coercion and needs a referral path rather than an exit.
ind.fp: Genuine emergency payments for relatives in legal or medical difficulty abroad, or legitimate bail and consular costs, can look similar.
ind.ds: Customers, often family members, send urgent payments abroad described as fees, fines or bail to secure the release of a relative who travelled for work, sometimes to many different recipient accounts or wallets.

ind.n: Business spend on telecoms, numbers, hosting or computing capacity out of line with its profile
ind.cx: Upstream footprint of the operation: payments for phone numbers, connectivity, hosting, cloud or computing capacity, advertising and unusually high electricity or internet bills.
ind.fp: Genuine call centres, data-heavy start-ups, crypto miners or marketing agencies.
ind.ds: A business or individual customer pays unusually large or recurring amounts for phone numbers, connectivity, domains, cloud or computing capacity, advertising or electricity that its stated activity does not explain.

ind.n: Virtual account numbers obscure which institution or account actually receives funds
ind.cx: Victim payments are collected through virtual account numbers (e.g. virtual IBANs) that hide the underlying account or institution.
ind.fp: Legitimate collection accounts used by payment providers and large billers.
ind.ds: Victim or customer payments go to virtual account identifiers (for example virtual IBANs) whose underlying holder or institution differs from what the payer was shown.

ind.n: One person holding multiple identities or accounts
ind.cx: Bought, sold or stolen identities used to open multiple accounts or wallets across providers, defeating name matching.
ind.fp: Customers may legitimately hold several products or use name variants; look for deliberate inconsistency.
ind.ds: The same individual appears under different names or opens several accounts or wallets, directly or through an intermediary.

ind.n: Stablecoins received from a DeFi service without AML controls, converted and withdrawn as fiat
ind.cx: Proceeds pass through DeFi services without AML controls and come back as stablecoins that are cashed out.
ind.fp: Legitimate DeFi yield or liquidity withdrawals by an established, documented customer.
ind.ds: Stablecoin deposits arrive from a decentralised service lacking AML/CFT controls and are promptly converted to fiat currency and withdrawn.

ind.n: Exposure to guarantee-marketplace wallets, tokens or shared infrastructure
ind.cx: Laundering through guarantee-marketplace infrastructure linked to scam centres.
ind.fp: Attribution lag or shared custodial infrastructure used by many unrelated services.
ind.ds: Direct or indirect transactions with addresses, tokens or address clusters attributed to, or sharing on-chain infrastructure with, a messaging-platform 'guarantee' (escrow) marketplace, with no apparent lawful purpose.

ind.n: Receiving exchange or remitter advertises 'no KYC' or claims false regulator approval
ind.cx: Victim funds sent to a remitter or exchange advertising 'no KYC' or a false regulator approval.
ind.fp: Marketing that refers accurately to a real registration or licence.
ind.ds: Open-source checks show the money service business or digital asset exchange receiving customer funds markets itself as needing no identity checks, or falsely claims it is approved by a regulator or FIU.

ctl.n: Funds hold, freeze and recall procedure
ctl.ds: Provides a defined, legally grounded capability to restrict, hold, freeze or recall funds and accounts pending review or on confirmed exposure, with clear triggers and approvers. It stops onward dissipation of suspected illicit funds.
Model that scores inbound-then-outbound pass-through, new-payee churn, counterparty diversity and profile mismatch to flag likely mule accounts. It prioritises accounts for review and restriction.

Investigates linked clusters and networks of accounts as one case, including broker networks and accounts connected to seizures or requests, rather than reviewing accounts individually. It disrupts organised activity that single-account review would miss.

ctl.n: Fan-in, fan-out and funnel account detection
ctl.ds: Detects accounts receiving from many unrelated senders, or sending to many beneficiaries, followed by consolidation or onward movement. It surfaces collector, funnel and mule structures.

ctl.n: Tightened monitoring for new accounts and entities
ctl.ds: Applies lower thresholds and closer review during the first months of an account or entity and alerts on turnover far above onboarding projections. It addresses the elevated risk at the start of a relationship.
Links accounts, devices, addresses, directors and beneficiaries to surface rings, shared attributes and flow structures that single-account views miss. It supports detection of organised networks.
Traces exposure of deposit and withdrawal addresses to illicit clusters and screens wallets with risk-scored alerts. It reveals on-chain exposure.

ctl.n: Counterparty VASP and platform due diligence
ctl.ds: Assesses the licensing, AML controls, jurisdiction and reputation of counterparty exchanges, over-the-counter desks and other virtual asset service providers before enabling flows, and reviews them periodically. It limits exposure through weak or complicit counterparties.

Fingerprints devices, IP addresses, emulators and network attributes to link applications, sessions and accounts and to flag shared or anomalous infrastructure. It exposes mule rings and multiple-account abuse.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.
Alerts when inflows are quickly moved out with little retained balance, including cash-in fast-out and rapid conversion or cash-out. It reveals accounts used as conduits for layering.
Flags direct and indirect exposure to mixers, privacy services and obfuscation tools against defined thresholds and applies enhanced review. It manages the traceability loss these tools create.

Compares actual activity with the customer's declared profile, history and peers and alerts on material or trend-breaking deviation, usually as a contextual signal. It catches change that rules on fixed thresholds miss.

Weights alert priority by the assessed risk of the counterparty and profiles counterparties that cannot be explained by the customer's business. It directs analyst attention to payments involving higher-risk parties.

Tests whether an entity has real operations such as premises, staff, stock and contracts through documents, site or virtual visits, open-source footprint and shell-risk indicators. It helps identify shell and front companies with no genuine activity.

Trains branch, contact-centre and relationship staff to ask open questions, recognise coaching, coercion, pressure and evasion and escalate with authority to pause. It strengthens the human control at the point of contact.

Provides discreet escalation routes and private conversation procedures so staff can refer suspected victims of exploitation, coercion or trafficking to specialists, police and support organisations. It prioritises victim safety.

Translates published and sanitised typologies and red flags into targeted monitoring scenarios and context-aware rules that are reviewed periodically. It aligns monitoring with known criminal methods.

Flags customers whose payments for telecoms numbers, connectivity, hosting, cloud or computing capacity, advertising and utilities are out of line with their stated business. It surfaces the upstream operating footprint of industrialised fraud operations that victim-side monitoring misses.
Restricts payable-through access or requires customer due diligence and monitoring at the sub-account holder level. It ensures third parties using a correspondent account are known and supervised.

ctl.n: Duplicate and synthetic identity checks at onboarding
ctl.ds: Compares new applicant identifiers such as name, email, phone, address, device and bank account with existing customers, previously declined or exited applicants and known-bad data. Matches are blocked or referred, limiting repeat applicants, synthetic identities and mule recruitment.

ctl.n: Dynamic payment friction and scam warnings
ctl.ds: Risk-scored payments trigger a purpose question and a tailored scam warning, or a call-back, before release to the customer. It gives the customer a chance to reconsider and interrupts payments made under deception.

Verifies licences, registrations and supervisory status of customers, agents and counterparties against regulator registers before onboarding and periodically. It confirms legal authority to operate and detects unlicensed activity.
